summary: Australian reviewers consistently praise the Inster's cleverly packaged, unexpectedly roomy cabin and its agile, fun-to-drive character in city conditions, with several noting it feels bigger inside than its tiny footprint suggests. Value remains the main criticism: even after the 2027 price cut to $37,500 before on-roads, the Inster sits well above the BYD Dolphin, and the cut came with the heat pump and interior V2L outlet deleted. The 2027 range is thinner, down to Standard Range and Cross after Hyundai dropped the Extended Range grade and the Cross roof-basket option, while interior plastics are widely described as hard and budget-grade and the rear bench seats only two.
pros: Cleverly packaged, surprisingly spacious cabin for such a small footprint, helped by sliding and fully-folding rear seats
Agile, easy-to-park city manners with light, precise steering
Efficient: 14.3 kWh/100km WLTP for the Standard Range, and CarExpert's tester saw 11.2 kWh/100km in mixed driving
Cross adds a 49 kWh battery for 360 km WLTP (vs 327 km), 17-inch alloys, heated and ventilated front seats and a surround-view camera
Hyundai extends the 5-year warranty to 7 years when every scheduled service is done at a Hyundai dealer; EV battery covered for 8 years/160,000 km
cons: Priced well above key budget-EV rivals such as the BYD Dolphin even after the 2027 cut to $37,500 (Standard Range) and $43,500 (Cross) before on-roads
Rear seating limited to two occupants, so four seats in total
2027 cars lose the heat pump, interior V2L outlet and emergency charging cable, which hurts winter range and versatility
Hard, budget-feeling interior plastics and a sparse rear row with no vents or USB outlets
Standard Range's 327 km WLTP is modest for anything beyond city and inner-suburban driving
